claim: Each AWS Region has at least three Availability Zones.
question: What is the minimum number of Availability Zones in an AWS Region?

values.spoken: at least three Availability Zones

qualifiers.condition: newer accounts can access two Availability Zones in US West (N. California)

evidence.quote: Each Region has at least three Availability Zones. This helps you to design highly available applications on AWS.

note: The same page has a footnote: newer accounts can access two Availability Zones in US West (N. California); writers should not say every account sees three AZs in every Region.

claim: An AZ ID such as use1-az1 names the same physical location in every AWS account, while an Availability Zone code such as us-east-1a can point to different physical locations in different accounts in the oldest Regions for accounts created before November 2025; use AZ IDs to line up Availability Zones across accounts.
question: What is the difference between an Availability Zone code and an AZ ID across accounts?

values.display: the same physical location in every AWS account
values.spoken: the same physical place in every account

values.display: might not be the same physical location
values.spoken: the zone letter can differ between accounts

qualifiers.scope: per Availability Zone, across AWS accounts
qualifiers.condition: independent code mapping applies in the oldest Regions for accounts created before November 2025

evidence.quote: For accounts created before November 2025, in our oldest Regions, we independently map Availability Zones to codes for each AWS account. For example, the `us-east-1a` Availability Zone for your account might not be the same physical location as it is in another account.
Each Availability Zone has an AZ ID, which is the same physical location in every AWS account.
For example, `use1-az1` is an AZ ID for the `us-east-1` Region, and it has the same physical location in every AWS account.

note: Accounts created starting November 2025 get the same mapping of codes; older exam questions assume codes differ per account.

claim: The Route 53 Resolver (Amazon DNS server) of a VPC is reachable at 169.254.169.253 over IPv4, at fd00:ec2::253 over IPv6, and at the primary private IPv4 CIDR range of the VPC plus two (for a 10.0.0.0/16 VPC, 10.0.0.2).
question: At which IP addresses can resources in a VPC reach the Amazon DNS server?

values.spoken: one sixty-nine dot two fifty-four dot one sixty-nine dot two fifty-three
the VPC base address plus two
ten dot zero dot zero dot two

qualifiers.condition: the plus-two address is in the primary IPv4 CIDR block

evidence.quote: The Route 53 Resolver is located at `169.254.169.253` (IPv4), `fd00:ec2::253` (IPv6), and at the primary private IPV4 CIDR range provisioned to your VPC plus two. For example, if you have a VPC with an IPv4 CIDR of `10.0.0.0/16` and an IPv6 CIDR of `2001:db8::/32`, you can reach the Route 53 Resolver at `169.254.169.253` (IPv4), `fd00:ec2::253` (IPv6), or `10.0.0.2` (IPv4).

claim: Each EC2 instance can send 1024 packets per second per network interface to Route 53 Resolver (the .2 address or 169.254.169.253), and this quota cannot be increased.
question: How many packets per second can an instance send to the Amazon DNS server, and can that be raised?

values.display: 1024 packets per second per network interface
values.spoken: one thousand twenty-four packets per second per network interface
it cannot be raised

qualifiers.scope: per network interface, per EC2 instance

evidence.quote: Each EC2 instance can send 1024 packets per second per network interface to Route 53 Resolver (specifically the .2 address, such as 10.0.0.2 and 169.254.169.253). This quota cannot be increased.

claim: A VPC IPv4 CIDR block can be between a /16 netmask (65,536 IP addresses) and a /28 netmask (16 IP addresses).
question: What is the largest and the smallest IPv4 CIDR block a VPC can have, in addresses?

values.spoken: slash sixteen, about sixty-five thousand addresses
slash twenty-eight, sixteen addresses

qualifiers.condition: /16 is the largest block and /28 the smallest

evidence.quote: When you create a VPC, you must specify an IPv4 CIDR block for the VPC. The allowed block size is between a `/16` netmask (65,536 IP addresses) and `/28` netmask (16 IP addresses).

claim: When a VPC has more than one subnet, the CIDR blocks of the subnets cannot overlap.
question: Can two subnets in the same VPC have overlapping CIDR blocks?

values.display: the CIDR blocks of the subnets cannot overlap
values.spoken: subnet ranges cannot overlap

evidence.quote: If you create more than one subnet in a VPC, the CIDR blocks of the subnets cannot overlap.

claim: A subnet CIDR block is either the same as the VPC CIDR block (one subnet for the whole VPC) or a subset of it (several subnets).
question: How must a subnet CIDR block relate to the VPC CIDR block?

values.display: the same as the CIDR block for the VPC
values.spoken: the same as the VPC range or a part of it

evidence.quote: The CIDR block of a subnet can be the same as the CIDR block for the VPC (to create a single subnet in the VPC), or a subset of the CIDR block for the VPC (to create multiple subnets in the VPC).

claim: In a 10.0.0.0/24 subnet AWS reserves five addresses: 10.0.0.0 is the network address, 10.0.0.1 is for the VPC router, 10.0.0.2 is for the DNS server, 10.0.0.3 is for future use, and 10.0.0.255 is the network broadcast address, reserved because a VPC does not support broadcast.
question: Which five addresses are reserved in a subnet, and what is each one for?

values.spoken: five reserved addresses

values.display: Reserved by AWS for the VPC router
values.spoken: the plus-one address is the VPC router

values.display: Reserved by AWS for future use
values.spoken: the plus-three address is for future use

values.display: We do not support broadcast in a VPC
values.spoken: the last address, because there is no broadcast

qualifiers.condition: example subnet 10.0.0.0/24; the pattern is the first four and the last address; not for BYOIP ranges

evidence.quote: The first four IP addresses and the last IP address in each subnet CIDR block are not available for your use, and they cannot be assigned to a resource, such as an EC2 instance. For example, in a subnet with CIDR block `10.0.0.0/24`, the following five IP addresses are reserved:
10.0.0.0: Network address.
10.0.0.1: Reserved by AWS for the VPC router.
10.0.0.2: Reserved by AWS. The IP address of the DNS server is the base of the VPC network range plus two.
10.0.0.3: Reserved by AWS for future use.
10.0.0.255: Network broadcast address. We do not support broadcast in a VPC, therefore we reserve this address.

claim: A /24 subnet has 256 IP addresses, of which 251 can be assigned to resources, because five addresses are reserved.
question: How many usable IP addresses does a /24 subnet have?

values.spoken: two hundred fifty-one usable addresses

qualifiers.condition: not for BYOIP ranges, where every address can be used

evidence.quote: For example, if you create a VPC with CIDR block `10.0.0.0/24`, it supports 256 IP addresses.
The first four IP addresses and the last IP address in each subnet CIDR block are not available for your use, and they cannot be assigned to a resource, such as an EC2 instance.

derivation: A /24 block holds 256 addresses (quote 1); the first four and the last are reserved (quote 2), so 256 - 5 = 251 can be assigned.

claim: In an IPv6 subnet the first four IPv6 addresses and the last IPv6 address of the subnet CIDR block are reserved and cannot be assigned to an EC2 instance.
question: Which addresses are reserved in an IPv6 subnet?

values.display: The first four IPv6 addresses and the last IPv6 address
values.spoken: the first four and the last IPv6 address

evidence.quote: The first four IPv6 addresses and the last IPv6 address in each subnet CIDR block are not available for your use, and they cannot be assigned to an EC2 instance.

claim: For an IPv4 range brought to AWS with BYOIP, you can use every address in the range, including the first (network) address and the last (broadcast) address.
question: Are the network and broadcast addresses reserved in a subnet that uses a BYOIP range?

values.display: you can use all of the IP addresses in the range
values.spoken: every address in a BYOIP range can be used

evidence.quote: If you bring an IPv4 address range to AWS using [BYOIP](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ec2-byoip.html), you can use all of the IP addresses in the range, including the first address (the network address) and the last address (the broadcast address).

claim: When you request an Amazon-provided IPv6 CIDR block for a VPC, Amazon provides a fixed block size of /56; for an IPv6 block from an IPAM pool or a BYOIP range, the possible netmask lengths are /44 to /60 in increments of /4.
question: What size is an Amazon-provided IPv6 CIDR block for a VPC?

values.spoken: a fixed slash fifty-six

qualifiers.scope: per Amazon-provided IPv6 CIDR block of a VPC
qualifiers.condition: Amazon-provided block; IPAM or BYOIP blocks can be /44 to /60 in increments of /4

evidence.quote: Amazon provides a fixed IPv6 CIDR block size of **/56**.
Possible IPv6 netmask lengths are between **/44** and **/60** in increments of /4.

note: The VPC FAQ still says a VPC IPv6 block is fixed at /56 and a subnet at /64 (facts vpc-faq-ipv6-vpc-fixed-56, vpc-faq-ipv6-subnet-fixed-64); the user guide (tier 1) allows /44 to /60 for VPCs and /44 to /64 for subnets since 2023-11. Teach the guide; /56 stays the Amazon-provided size.
